https://www.arbuturian.com/travel/travel.text: Trending Getting High in Haute-Savoie A Lunch with…Matthew Jukes Willett’s Nirvana Mediterranean Excellence: Reframing the All-Inclusive Up on the Hill: A Night Beneath the Chiltern Stars Roast in Peace: A Sunday at The Mutton Richard Dadd: A Much-Respected Murderer El Fuerte: Marbella’s Grand Dame, Reimagined Cooper’s Cut Ariadne auf Naxos at Glyndebourne M.C.Escher: The Exhibition Spa of the Month: Bellevue, Lošinj By Toby 'Lawrence' White on July 18, 2026 Travel In a distant corner of the Adriatic, once the Habsburgs’ cure for what ailed them, Larry checks into the boutique Hotel Alhambra, on an island that got there before wellness was a word… Technically, we’re in Istria. It’s a misty drive through pine-dressed mountains, terracotta rooftops, villages in various states of restoration and repose, and glimpses down to the sea. Losinj itself is something of a schlep, from anywhere, but I’ve written many a tome in these pages about the pleasure being in the journey, and the joys of losing yourself in a distant, discoverable part of the world. From Pula, we get our first glimpse of the destination as we round the top of the mainland, down to the ferry that carries us across to the islands. Once over the strait, it’s an hour down the length of Cres, the mountains taper into rolling heathland, through villages like Osor, from which we cross the smallest of bridges onto Losinj itself. We’re headed to Čikat Bay, a small cove on the far side of a narrow isthmus shaping a long natural harbour into Mali Losinj, the island’s largest town — though that rather overstates it. Here, cradled in pine woodland at the water’s edge, sits Hotel Alhambra; three buildings, two of them former villas — the oldest dating to 1908 — bookending a more contemporary addition. It’s part of a wider estate, Losinj Hotels & Villas, arranged around the bay to take in the sleeker Bellevue and five fin-de-siècle villas besides. With a scattering of independent cafés, eateries and activity outfits along the waterfront, it has all the benefits of a resort, just without the whiff of entrapment. Looking at this setting, I’m intrigued as to how these grand, palatial houses — now fitted out with mind-bogglingly stunning interiors — ever came to be here, in this distant, even remote corner of Croatia. The answer would come the next morning. For now, I was happy enough simply settling into this slice of idyll. Inside, the design is contemporary and eclectic, without losing its sense of history; stylised artworks show the villas in yesteryear, butting against striking modern fixtures, captured against the backdrop of the buildings’ original features. One minute you can be looking onto the bay through wraparound floor-to-ceiling windows in the lobby, then you turn a corner and enter the wood-panelled library, enjoying petit fours, served every tea time. My room is in one of the older buildings, so it keeps a number of original features. Perhaps the most striking touch, besides the double-height ceiling, is a bathroom that opens straight onto the terrace. There are lovely details, too; the motion sensor light in the walk-in wardrobe, the mood lighting, the TV speakers built into the bathroom mirror — useful when not wishing to miss the news while preparing for dinner. That evening, at Alfred Keller, Alhambra’s Michelin-starred restaurant, I crack the wax seal on a menu billed as three courses that amounts to nearer eight. I’m not sure why I should be surprised to find exceptional cuisine tucked into a secluded cove on this distant stretch of the Adriatic — Michelin reaches most corners of the world these days — but I was. Snacks alongside a Slavonian barrel-aged negroni ran to a parmesan and truffle croquette, presented as a black truffle on a bed of moss, and bacon-wrapped asparagus with goat’s cheese foam. The highlight, though, was the kingfish — flambéed, the waiter told me, a technique I thought had gone out with the ’70s — in a tangy tomato consommé with pickled fennel. There are joys, too, among the wines. A sparkling Tomac, rivalling anything southeast England might produce, would become a new regular aperitif on my visit. Being in such a pine-rich, picturesque setting rather infuses one with a desire to embrace nature. In my case, quite literally. The spa offers rituals of an arboreal bent, so, duly fortified with a hot ginger and lemon before breakfast, I’m out into the woods for a mindful ‘breathing’ session among the trees. A shoreline promenade runs not just around Čikat Bay but much of the island, and it’s here, walking through the pines with the sea lapping just feet away, that you get a real sense of place. It is, entirely, serene. I pass jasmine and am awash with scent. The island’s restorative reputation, it turns out, is not just hokum. On this meandering walk I learn why the villas exist here at all. Under the Austro-Hungarian empire, Losinj became known as a health resort, thanks largely to the botanist Ambroz Haračić — commemorated with a statue in the bay — who catalogued the island’s flora while searching for a cure for his son’s asthma. Word spread, and soon the Habsburgs’ glitterati were building palatial holiday homes in this botanically rich corner of the empire. A handful of those properties have since become Alhambra and its villas, and staying in them, I confess to feeling ever so slightly imperious myself, lordly parading down to the seafront in my bathrobe. Even today, with 1,200 plant species and its agreeable climate, Losinj ranks among the most botanically wealthy islands in the Mediterranean, a legacy the hotel’s spa captures with an “inhalation bar” — its take on a respiratory tonic that dates to 1892, when aristocratic visitors would stop at the island’s Kurhaus to breathe in mists of seawater and medicinal aerosols. Waiting for my therapist and a signature herbal massage, I find the modern equivalent: an antique cabinet housing a bulbous ceramic vessel from which one inhales plant-infused sea air. Perhaps more psychosomatic than efficacious, but between the botanical walk, the cold sea plunges from the sundecks and a lungful of resin-scented air at every turn, I was beginning to feel thoroughly, if implausibly, cured. It wouldn’t be Croatia without getting out on the water, and this being a lesser-known region, there are some genuinely untapped spots left to find. Sailing might be the purist’s choice, but without the luxury of time, a powerboat — sun deck, naturally — is the more efficient option. We skip across to Susak, visible from Losinj, for a spot of exploratory beachcombing. It has a population today of barely 150 — a small port village, a church and a lighthouse marking its highest points — and crossing the water towards it feels rather like crossing time. Before the war, the population was closer to 1,600, ten times its current size, and the island lived on wine; when the new communist government taxed the trade into oblivion, the islanders left, most of them for Hoboken, New Jersey. But, remarkably, their descendants still return every summer. More developed is Ilovik, tucked into Losinj’s tail and known as the ‘Island of Flowers’ for its own abundance of oleander, rose and eucalyptus. Heading back up the coast to Mali Losinj, I find it remarkable that a stretch of the Mediterranean this handsome hasn’t been given over to wall-to-wall hotels. What stays with me most is the colour of the water — the Adriatic has a shade of blue entirely its own. A hundred yards up the promenade, in some contrast to Alhambra, sits the larger, more contemporary Bellevue. Here, in the spirit of the sea’s bounty, we dine at Matsunoki, the group’s award-laden Japanese restaurant. After a run of tasting starters — Kobe beef fukuju, beef tataki with truffle mayonnaise, duck gyoza, tuna tartare — comes a sashimi course of remarkable range: sea bass, a volcano tuna roll, golden dragon, wagyu asparagus, plus salmon, hamachi and tuna sashimi, alongside an exquisite 40%-polished Fukujo ‘blue’ sake. Ironically, for all that dazzling fish, the highlight turns out to be the simplicity of a miso ice cream for dessert, even upstaging the strudel-like apple gyoza it accompanies. It’s hard to leave Alhambra without feeling that the whole place is, in some sense, still practising what those nineteenth-century botanists preached. The pines that shelter it, the sea that laps at its jetty, the very air one is encouraged to breathe more deeply — none of it is incidental; it’s the point, and has been for well over a century. Other hotels borrow the language of wellness. Alhambra simply inherited it, along with the villas, the woodland and the view. A heritage of healing, a legacy of luxury, as they put it themselves — and, for once, the strapline undersells it. I came in search of nothing more than a good story and a decent dinner. I left rather wondering whether I’d been cured of something I hadn’t known was wrong with me. For more information about Boutique Hotel Alhambra, including details of other properties in the portfolio, please visit www.boutiquehotelalhambra.com . And for a deeper dive into breathing therapies and their spa’s signature Seatox programme, have a look at Anna Selby’s ‘Spa of the Month’ feature on the Bellevue here . Share. https://english.news.cn/20260903/30d65d5.text: Estonian defense minister announces resignation over audit findings Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-03 03:53:30 TALLINN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur announced his resignation on Wednesday, saying he was taking political responsibility after the National Audit Office found serious problems in the management and accounting of the country's defense sector. Pevkur, who has served as defense minister since 2022, announced his decision during a live broadcast of "Aktuaalne kaamera," the flagship evening news program of Estonian public broadcaster ERR. He said he considered it right to assume political responsibility for the entire defense sector and would hand over his duties when Prime Minister Kristen Michal considered it appropriate. The National Audit Office said last week that serious deficiencies in the Defense Forces' inventory accounting meant auditors could not establish the accuracy of an inventory balance of about 1.2 billion euros (about 1.4 billion U.S. dollars). The auditors also identified shortcomings in contract management, monitoring of contract performance, and procedures for verifying and recording goods received. Estonia has sharply increased defense spending in recent years. The country's defense expenditure is set at 5.4 percent of gross domestic product in 2026, compared with about 3.3 percent in 2025, according to the Defense Ministry. ■

Our Heritage GX94 App Apple App Store Google Play Contact Us Advertise Courtesy of Orano Facebook Saskatchewan’s nuclear capacity takes centre stage in the United Kingdom By SaskToday Sep 5, 2026 | 5:00 PM REGINA, Sask. — Premier Scott Moe is leading a trade and investment mission to the United Kingdom (U.K.) to reinforce Saskatchewan's position as the jurisdiction of choice in nuclear co-operation, states Sask. Trade and Export Development in a press release. Moe will participate in the World Nuclear Symposium and Canada – U.K. Nuclear Day. Minister of Crown Investments Corporation Jeremy Harrison will join the World Nuclear Symposium after representing Saskatchewan at the MSPO Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland alongside federal and provincial counterparts. "Our province has what it takes to be a world leader in nuclear energy development with our extensive uranium resources, nuclear research infrastructure and supply chain capabilities, and Saskatchewan-based businesses and research organizations are at the forefront of the global nuclear renaissance," Moe said. "The U.K. has been a vital gateway to growing Saskatchewan's nuclear sector and I look forward to building on our relationships. After all, it is these relationships that help bring home investment, jobs and reinforce Saskatchewan as a leader in the world's energy future." "Saskatchewan is uniquely positioned to support the next generation of nuclear development around the world," Harrison said. "From our world-class uranium resources to our expertise across the nuclear sector, we have what the world needs. This mission showcases our strengths, deepens relationships with industry and government leaders and creates new opportunities for Saskatchewan's nuclear sector." The World Nuclear Symposium drew more than 1,100 participants from 59 countries in 2025. Moe will be participating in a panel event profiling Saskatchewan's nuclear ecosystem. Canada-U.K. Nuclear Day will feature keynote discussions and expert panels from across the nuclear sector. Moe, alongside Cameco and the Saskatchewan First Nations Centre of Excellence will represent Saskatchewan. Over the past five years, Saskatchewan's exports to the U.K. increased by 177.9 per cent, from $211.5 million in 2021 to $587.6 million in 2025. This growth has been driven by uranium exports, which in 2025 accounted for 57.1 per cent of the province's total U.K. exports. In the same five-year period, the value of exports to Poland have increased by 3,503 per cent, from $2.2 million in 2021 to $79 million in 2025. This growth is mainly due to potash exports. Saskatchewan operates a trade and investment office in London. For more information on Saskatchewan's international network, visit: InvestSK.ca . https://neweasterneurope.eu/2026/09/25/r.text: Russia and North Korea open a new route for their wartime partnership Satellite imagery and Russian procurement records illustrate the scale of new freight infrastructure on the border, as Moscow and Pyongyang deepen military cooperation during the war in Ukraine. September 25, 2026 - Ana Pisarenco - Analysis The new road crossing between Khasan in Russia’s Far East and Tumangang in North Korea. Photograph: Ministry of Transport of the Russian Federation Inside this article Russia and North Korea opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River on September 7th 2026, establishing a new land route to support freight transport and logistics. Experts link the new road crossing to deepening military cooperation and the need to improve logistics for equipment and supplies amid Russia's war against Ukraine. The deepening military alliance between Moscow and Pyongyang, including North Korean troop deployments and weapons transfers, raises significant security concerns for Seoul, Washington, and European nations. Russia and North Korea opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River on September 7th 2026, giving the two countries a new land route as their military relationship deepens during Russia’s war against Ukraine. Trucks began using the crossing for freight the same day. The bridge is only part of what has been built. Sentinel-2 imagery analysed for this article and Russian procurement records show a much larger border-processing project around the crossing. An approximate measurement using Copernicus Browser put the principal developed area on the Russian side at about 18 hectares, compared with roughly five hectares on the North Korean side. The Khasan checkpoint is initially designed to handle 300 vehicles a day, with capacity planned to rise to as many as 800. Oleksandr Danylyuk, chairman of the Kyiv-based Center for Defence Reforms and an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), said the new crossing gives the two countries another logistics option. He previously served as chief adviser to Ukraine’s defence minister, special adviser to the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service and assistant to the commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces. “They had this one railroad only, and they need to have some other options,” Danylyuk said in an interview. Russia and North Korea already had the railway crossing at Khasan and Tumangang, alongside maritime routes connecting North Korea with ports in Russia’s Far East. Danylyuk linked the additional road connection to military cooperation and the equipment Russia receives from North Korean factories. “They need to improve logistics for these purposes, to support each other militarily,” he said. Sentinel-2 imagery cannot establish whether North Korean weapons are being transported across the bridge. With its resolution, individual vehicles and their cargo cannot be identified reliably. In 2024, Russia and North Korea signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty containing a mutual defence provision. North Korean troops were later deployed to support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Built for more traffic Construction around the crossing can be followed through satellite imagery. Sentinel-2 images reviewed for this article show extensive changes on both sides of the Tumen River between June 2025 and July 2026. By March 2026, the bridge alignment was visibly continuous. By July, substantial processing areas and road infrastructure were visible on both banks. Sentinel-2 imagery shows the road crossing and border infrastructure at Khasan and Tumangang before and after the bridge opened. Images: Copernicus Sentinel data 2026, processed with Copernicus Browser. Analysis and approximate measurements by the author. The measurements were made by tracing the principal developed areas visible in Copernicus Browser. They are approximate visual estimates rather than cadastral boundaries. Russian procurement documents demonstrate for what the infrastructure is intended. Plans for Khasan describe four freight lanes, two bus lanes, two passenger-car lanes and two reserve lanes, alongside separate passenger and freight-processing buildings, passport and customs facilities, quarantine functions, vehicle inspection points and deep-inspection bays. The new road crossing runs alongside the existing rail connection between Khasan and Tumangang. Border-processing infrastructure is visible on both sides of the Tumen River. Image: Copernicus Sentinel data 2026, processed with Copernicus Browser. Russia has also announced upgrades to more than 100 kilometres of road towards Vladivostok, connecting the crossing with the wider road network in Primorsky Krai. A Sentinel-2 image from September 12th, five days after the opening, shows the completed crossing and facilities on both sides. Most of the major supporting infrastructure visible in September was already in place by July. The wartime relationship Han Ki-bum spent more than two decades analysing North Korea inside South Korea’s National Intelligence Service. From 2013 to 2016, he served as the agency’s first deputy director, responsible for North Korean and overseas affairs. He is now an adjunct senior fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies. Han has said relations with Russia changed markedly in 2023. What had largely been an exchange of North Korean weapons and ammunition for foreign currency and food widened into summits, a new treaty, troop deployments and contacts across the two governments. Han described the process as institutionalization, although he does not consider it complete. Political decisions in Moscow and Pyongyang still drive much of the relationship, while the war has accelerated it. He expects the road to increase exchanges between North Korea and Russia’s Primorsky Krai, but doubts it will produce a dramatic rise in trade. North Korea’s industrial system remains heavily dependent on China, Han said. Its economic compatibility with Russia is weaker, Moscow is farther away and the Russian Far East offers a much smaller economic base than north-eastern China. He cautioned against treating the new Russian crossing as equivalent to North Korea’s major bridge links with China. Han considers Russian assistance in some areas of conventional weapons development highly plausible. He pointed to drones and air-defence systems, two areas in which North Korea has had weaknesses. Some improvements, he said, have subsequently appeared in equipment displayed by Pyongyang. He is more cautious about advanced missile and nuclear technology. Russia has an immediate reason to help improve North Korean short-range ballistic missiles used under battlefield conditions, Han said. Evidence for transfers involving longer-range systems, warships or the strategic development of North Korea’s nuclear programme is less conclusive. Lessons from the battlefield North Korean forces are gaining battlefield experience in Ukraine. Han cautioned against assuming that all of it could be transferred directly to the Korean peninsula. Western Russia has extensive open terrain; Korea is mountainous. Climate and geography would shape combat differently. He identified drone warfare, artillery and missile operations, air defence, communications and command systems as areas where experience gained in Ukraine could improve North Korean forces. Closer ties with Moscow have also weakened the international framework built to constrain Pyongyang, Han said. Russia’s approach to UN sanctions and its military relationship with North Korea have made efforts towards de-nuclearisation more difficult. North and South Korea remain technically at war, Danylyuk noted, while the United States has a treaty commitment to defend the South. “It should be a matter of concern for South Korea, for sure,” he said. Danylyuk, meanwhile, sees Russia’s military alliance with Pyongyang as a direct security concern for Seoul and Washington. North Korean troops and weapons are being used in Europe, while Pyongyang is gaining military experience and receiving Russian support. From Korea to the Black Sea Romania’s defence relationship with South Korea has moved from weapons purchases towards local production. Tudor Curtifan, editor-in-chief of DefenseRomania and a Romanian defence and foreign-policy analyst, points to Bucharest’s 2024 contract for Hanwha Aerospace’s K9 Thunder self-propelled howitzers. Romania ordered 54 K9 systems, with 36 due to be produced locally. Hanwha is also developing a plant at Petrești, in Dâmbovița county. Curtifan said Russia’s invasion accelerated a relationship that predates the war. Romania and South Korea established a strategic partnership in 2008. The deployment of North Korean troops in Ukraine has added a new security dimension. “The internationalization of the war by the Russian Federation, with the presence of North Korean troops on the Ukrainian front, has made the geostrategic interests of the two states intersect even more,” Curtifan said. “East Asia and Eastern Europe are much closer strategically than they are geographically.” In addition to Romania, Poland has become an even larger European example of defence-industrial cooperation with South Korea. Both countries sits on NATO’s Eastern Flank, next to Ukraine, where North Korean troops have fought alongside Russian forces. Beyond the war Han does not expect relations between Moscow and Pyongyang to return to where they were before the war. Russia could still use North Korean labour during reconstruction, he said, while Pyongyang would have reasons to preserve Russian economic and military assistance and Moscow’s diplomatic support. As long as Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un remain in power, he considers a rapid deterioration in relations unlikely. China’s economic weight and proximity will continue to limit how far Russia can displace it. Han expects some loosening if the war ends and Russia’s reconstruction needs eventually decline. Moscow could remain substantially more important to Pyongyang than it was before 2022 without replacing China or sustaining the present intensity of military cooperation. The new bridge adds a road connection to the railway and maritime routes the two countries already use. Russian documents show a crossing designed for freight and higher traffic. Satellite imagery shows the infrastructure built around it, but not what cargo will dominate the route. Ana Pisarenco is a journalist based in Moldova.
